# Book III, Proposition 19

*The centre is on the straight line at right angles to the tangent*

> If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/19-idea.svg" alt="At the point where a straight line touches the circle (red), stand a straight line at right angles to it (yellow): it runs through the centre (black)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>At the point where a straight line touches the circle (red), stand a straight line at right angles to it (yellow): it runs through the centre (black).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/19.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.19, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let a straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, and from C let CA be drawn at right angles to DE;

I say that the centre of the circle is on AC.

For suppose it is not, but, if possible, let F be the centre,

and let CF be joined.

Since a straight line DE touches the circle ABC,

and FC has been joined from the centre to the point of contact,

FC is perpendicular to DE; [III. 18]

therefore the angle FCE is right.

But the angle ACE is also right;

therefore the angle FCE is equal to the angle ACE,

the less to the greater: which is impossible.

Therefore F is not the centre of the circle ABC.

Similarly we can prove that neither is any other point except a point on AC.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop19.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop19.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at
right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn. -/
theorem Prop19 {A C D E : Point} {ABC : Circle} (hC : OnCircle C ABC) (hDE : Touches D E ABC)
    (hCDE : Collinear D E C) (hA : ¬ Collinear D E A)
    (hCA : ∀ P : Point, Collinear D E P → P ≠ C → ∠ A C P = ∟) :
    ∀ F : Point, Centre F ABC → Collinear A C F := by
  -- For let a straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, and from C let CA be drawn
  -- at right angles to DE;
  obtain ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE.1
  have hC_L : OnLine C L := by
    obtain ⟨M, h1, h2, h3⟩ := hCDE
    exact (line_unique hDE.1 h1 h2 hD_L hE_L) ▸ h3
  have hA_L : ¬ OnLine A L := fun h => hA ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L, h⟩
  /- Euclid's `E` is a point of `DE` other than `C`: `E` itself, or `D` when `C` is `E`. -/
  obtain ⟨E₁, hE₁_L, hE₁C⟩ : ∃ E₁ : Point, OnLine E₁ L ∧ E₁ ≠ C := by
    by_cases hCE : C = E
    · exact ⟨D, hD_L, fun e => hDE.1 (e.trans hCE)⟩
    · exact ⟨E, hE_L, Ne.symm hCE⟩
  -- I say that the centre of the circle is on AC.
  intro F hF
  -- For suppose it is not, but, if possible, let F be the centre,
  refine Classical.byContradiction fun hF_AC => ?_
  -- and let CF be joined.
  have hF_L : ¬ OnLine F L := fun h => hDE.not_inside ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L, h⟩ (centre_inside hF)
  -- Since a straight line DE touches the circle ABC,
  -- and FC has been joined from the centre to the point of contact,
  -- FC is perpendicular to DE; [III. 18]
  have h18 := Prop18 hF hC hDE hCDE
  -- therefore the angle FCE is right.
  have hFCE : ∠ F C E₁ = ∟ := h18 E₁ ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L, hE₁_L⟩ hE₁C
  -- But the angle ACE is also right;
  have hACE : ∠ A C E₁ = ∟ := hCA E₁ ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L, hE₁_L⟩ hE₁C
  -- therefore the angle FCE is equal to the angle ACE,
  have hFCE_ACE : ∠ F C E₁ = ∠ A C E₁ := hFCE.trans hACE.symm
  -- the less to the greater: which is impossible.
  /- One ray from `C` on `F`'s side of `DE` makes a right angle with it (`onRay_of_angle_eq`).
     Euclid's figure has `F` on `A`'s side; on the other side, `AC` produced to `A₁`. -/
  have hFC : F ≠ C := fun e => hF_L (e ▸ hC_L)
  have hAC : A ≠ C := fun e => hA_L (e ▸ hC_L)
  have hEq : ∠ E₁ C F = ∠ E₁ C A := by
    rw [angle_symm hE₁C hFC, angle_symm hE₁C hAC]; exact hFCE_ACE
  obtain ⟨M, hA_M, hC_M⟩ := Postulate1 A C hAC
  apply hF_AC
  by_cases hs : SameSide F A L
  · obtain ⟨-, -, ⟨N, hC_N, hA_N, hF_N⟩, -⟩ :=
      onRay_of_angle_eq (SameSideOf.of_line hE₁C.symm hC_L hE₁_L hs) hEq
    exact ⟨N, hA_N, hC_N, hF_N⟩
  · obtain ⟨A₁, hA₁_M, hCA₁, -⟩ := Postulate2 hA_M hC_M hAC []
    have hE₁_M : ¬ OnLine E₁ M := fun h =>
      hA_L ((line_unique hE₁C.symm hC_M h hC_L hE₁_L) ▸ hA_M)
    have hA₁_L : ¬ OnLine A₁ L := fun h =>
      hA_L (on_line_of_between (between_symm hCA₁) h hC_L)
    have hadj := adjacent_eq_of_right hA_M hA₁_M hCA₁ hE₁_M hACE
    have hEq₁ : ∠ E₁ C F = ∠ E₁ C A₁ := by
      rw [hEq, angle_symm hE₁C hAC, hadj]
    have hFA₁ : SameSide F A₁ L := same_side_of_opposite_sides
      ⟨hA_L, hF_L, fun h => hs (same_side_symm h)⟩ ⟨hA_L, hA₁_L, pasch3 hCA₁ hC_L⟩
    obtain ⟨-, -, ⟨N, hC_N, hA₁_N, hF_N⟩, -⟩ :=
      onRay_of_angle_eq (SameSideOf.of_line hE₁C.symm hC_L hE₁_L hFA₁) hEq₁
    have hNM : N = M := line_unique (ne_of_between (between_symm hCA₁)).symm hC_N hA₁_N hC_M hA₁_M
    subst hNM
    exact ⟨N, hA_M, hC_N, hF_N⟩
  -- Therefore F is not the centre of the circle ABC.
  -- Similarly we can prove that neither is any other point except a point on AC.
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**The centre has nowhere else to go.** Euclid turns III.18 into a way of finding where the centre lies. CA is drawn at right angles to DE at C; were the centre a point F off CA, the straight line FC would make a second right angle with DE, by III.18. But two straight lines from C on one side of DE cannot both be at right angles to it: the angle FCE would be equal to the angle ACE, "the less to the greater". Like Heath, we draw F off AC, inside the angle ACE, where the supposition puts it.

**A converse left over.** Heath goes on counting after III.18: "We may also regard III. 19 as a partial converse of III. 18" (vol. 2, p. 45). Now the three things are a straight line through the centre, one through the point of contact, and one perpendicular to the tangent. III.18 gives the third from the first two, and III.19 gives the first from the last two. The pairing left over is a converse Euclid does not state: "a straight line drawn through the centre perpendicular to the tangent passes through the point of contact" (vol. 2, p. 46).

**Which side of DE?** Our statement asks less of A than Heath's figure does. A is any point off DE with CA at right angles to it, not necessarily on the circle, and so it may lie on the other side of DE from the centre. Then we produce AC beyond C (Postulate 2), and the angle there is right too, so the straight line at right angles reaches F's side after all. On one side of DE only one ray from C makes a right angle with it (`onRay_of_angle_eq`), and that is Euclid's "the less to the greater": an angle cannot be equal to a part of itself.

**The modern way.** For a nonzero tangent direction v, III.18 gives (C − F)·v = 0. Through C there is one straight line perpendicular to v: X = C + s(C − F), which passes through the centre F at s = −1.
